speakeroldname: Hon. C. C. BALLANTYNE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
without wishing to detain the members of the Committee, I think it might be interesting to hon. members if I made a very brief reference to the fisheries of Canada and to the reorganization that it is proposed to put into effect. In order that I may be accurate, if hon. members will allow me I will read this brief memorandum that I have here and then they will better understand the Estimates which will be placed before them for consideration.
Reorganization of the Outside Service has not yet been effected, but a method of doing

so has been worked out and approved by the Civil Service Commission. As soon as reclassification of salaries has been completed, steps will be taken to put the reorganization into effect. It is anticipated that the reorganized service will be in complete working order by the end of this calendar year. In broad lines, the reorgtanization will be as follows:
For the purposes of Fisheries administration, Chnada will be divided into three sections, the fisheries of each of which are common in their character, viz:-The Atlantic Provinces ; The Prairie Provinces ; British Columbia.
Ontario and Quebec, so far as their inland waters are concerned, administer their own fisheries.
To assure the greatest possible co-ordination of the administrative service and the closest and most direct supervision, and at the same time to provide that those engaging in the industry may be in the closest possible contact with the Department, each of these sections will be placed under the charge of a Chief Inspector of Fisheries, through whose office all the work of that division will ibe carried on. District Inspectors will be continued as at present. Local overseers will be employed, but instead of having a large number of them with small districts and insignificant salaries, so that they must engage in other work to make a living, each overseer will have as large a district als he can efficiently handle, and he will be require-' to devote his whole time and attention to his work. He will be paid a reasonable salary. The amount has not yet been fixed by the Commission.
Special guardian's will have to be employed in some instances at certain times of the year, particularly to protect fish on the spawning grounds in the rivers. But no greater number of such guardians will be employed than is absolutely necessary, and then only for such limited period as their services are really needed. In any instances where services are required for more than thirty days, advertisements will be published calling for applications for the position.
The lobster catch for 1918 fell very much below that for 1(917. In fact it was little more than half the annual average of the catch of the four preceding years. This sharp decline should not, however, be too readily attributed to a scarcity of lobsters. The falling off was common on all parts of the coast, and a strong contributing cause will be found in the protracted spells of stormy weather and1 the abnormal ice conditions that prevailed last spring.
The total value of our fisheries for 1917 amounted to $52,312,044. This sum is more than $13,000,000 greater than the value of the fisheries for the previous year.
This brief statement will give hon. members some, idea of what we are going to do. As we proceed with the Estimates I shall be very glad to give any further information that may be required.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Are new inspectors to be appointed to these new positions that are to be created? What will be their salaries. What commission does my hon. friend refer to when he says that the " commission " has not decided on the salary?

, Mr. BALLANTYNE: We have a Chief Inspector of Fisheries in British Columbia, Colonel Cunningham, whose headquarters are at Vancouver. It will be necessary to appoint also a Chief Inspector for the Maritime Provinces. All such appointments will, of course, be made by the Civil Service Commission. The salary of Colonel Cunningham, whose responsibilities out there are very heavy and who has been with the department for many years, is *54,000 a year.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: A large deputation waited on the minister recently and suggested some changes in the organization of the department. May I ask whether any progress has been made? Is that matter still under consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Fielding) was present when the delegation from the Canadian Fisheries Association waited upon me. Some of the suggestions that this association made have already been acted upon. In my Supplementary Estimates I intend to ask for an amount for fishing tugs to patrol Lake Erie and to replace the steamer Vigilant, which formerly did that work. That was one of the suggestions that the association made. The most important suggestion that they made was that the fisheries of Canada should be in charge of a deputy minister who would give his whole time to that work, and that the present able deputy, Mr. Des-barats, should not act as deputy minister both for the Fisheries Branch and the Naval Service Branch. I agree with that recommendation, and I hope that before the next session of 'Parliament we shall have a deputy minister who will devote all his time to the fisheries. We intend also to employ a man who will give most of his time to the commercial side of the question, to the marketing of fish, and so on. The man I am looking for will be a bright young business man who will be able to study the markets of Canada as well as markets abroad, to look into the transportation question, and to advise the deputy minister and myself. While the volume of the fisheries of Canada is very large, a great deal more can be done, and now that the war is over an even more vigorous policy will be pursued than has been followed in past years.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Is the $100,000 increase chiefly for increased salaries and additional salaries to new appointees?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
The appropriation is to provide for the necessary extensions of

the service and for the reorganization to which I have referred; also, for salaries and for the appointment of further fishery officers. When my fishery Estimates were before the Committee last year I said that the number of guardians would be very much reduced. I am glad to inform the Committee that this has been done. In 1917 there were 806 guardians throughout Canada; during the past year that number has been reduced to 392, and we have employed them only for the length of time that we wanted them-for one month or two months, as the case might be. Their remuneration has been increased, and we ask that the service rendered be much better- in fact, that it be such as the appointments call for. Therefore, while the number of guardians has been reduced the remuneration to them has been increased, but the cost on the whole has been lessened. The total cost for guardians in 1917 was $94,290.59, and this year, with an increased remuneration to guardians, it is only $80,818.78.
iMr. McKENZIE:	I understand that a
new inspector is to be appointed for the Maritime Provinces. Is this appointment for the three Maritime Provinces, or is it only for one? What would the specific duties of this new official be?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Only one Superintendent of Fisheries will be appointed for all the Maritime Provinces, and it will be his duty to co-ordinate the work, to have full charge of the overseers and also of the guardians, and in a general way to be responsible to the department at Ottawa for all of the Maritime fisheries. I think such an appointment will prove to be a good one. It has worked so in British Columbia, and since I have had the honour of being Minister of Fisheries, I have done my utmost to run the department free from politics and to put it on a good business basis. I do not claim to have done wonders, but my sincere desire is to get the best men we can, and to place the fisheries of Canada on an even better footing than at present and to expand them*.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The minister has stated that he is looking for salesmen in the interests o*f the fisheries of the country. Has he in mind that the increased expenditure will in any way reduce the high cost of living, or if it will decrease the price of fish to the Canadian consumer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I have in mind just exactly what the hon. member has, namely,
that we shall induce the public to eat more fish, and I hope the cost of fish will also go down. The problem is, however, a very large one.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: What are the minister's hopes based on?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: On this, that we are going to have a publicity department and to do far more advertising than has been done in the past. We intend getting out very attractive booklets about the various kinds of fish, how they may be cooked, how palatable they are and all that sort of thing, just the same as a live business concern would do. We also hope to have more steam trawlers put in use than there are in use at present, and as the volume of the output of the fisheries of Canada is increased, the cost ought to decline. But I will make no promises in that regard, because the problem is too* big a one for a minister to state definitely that he can reduce the cost. We will do everything we can to reduce it, and we can only hope we shall be successful.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I -should like to know
whether the Government or the minister in charge has in mind the high cost of living in this country. Every minister who has brought up his Estimates so far has had an increase in them. The minister now tells us that he has cut off some 400 inspectors and other employees of one kind or another, and yet in face of that he is asking us for an increased expenditure of $100,000. Every minister seems to be heading in the same direction of in-10 p.m. creased expenditure and of making positions for his friends. New positions in unlimited numbers are being created from day to day, but so far no minister has told us that he is endeavouring to decrease the cost of living, or that he is thinking at all about the people. It is all very well for us to vote away the people's money, $600,000 in salaries including an increase of $100,000 over last year, which will in all probability increase the -cost of living to the Canadian consumer, and the minister -tells us frankly that he has in mind no plan that will decrease the cost. It would be very much better -for the Government to spend that $100,000 in endeavouring to find some way of furnishing fish to the Canadian consumer at lower prices than those of to-day. But if the Government wishes to consider only the commercial interests of the country, without any regard to the consuming

public, we shall continue along in the same direction in which we are now going and get in deeper all the time. All the Government seems to have in mind is to spend money to do business, but that money has to be paid some day, and the ministers should turn their attention to the high cost of living and endeavour to reduce it to the poor people of this country instead of providing what are apparently political jobs for their friends. I take the minister's word when he says he is not letting politics enter into this thing, but apparently, all the ministers say the same thing and they have all found a way of creating new positions at high salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I should not want the hon. member to think that this expenditure is for fishery officers alone; it is for the fishery patrol service and for oyster culture. It might interest the hon. member to know that the price of fish has very materially dropped since the armistice was signed, but I do not take any credit for that. If this new general sales manager, or publicity man, or whatever you like to call him, is the kind of man I hope we shall get, he will be able to look into transportation charges and all that kind of thing in order that fish may be delivered to fish dealers at the lowest possible cost. It is quite probable that the cost of fish will continue to go down, and we want to take advantage of meat unfortunately being as high as it is and fish low to increase the consumption of fish and to educate the people more in the use of it. As regards the consumer, the hon member will, I am sure, understand that I as well as every other member on this side of the House have the consumer in mind as much as our friends on the other side. No one knows that better than my genial friend the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), who knows that the consumer is always the apple of our eye.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The curious feature of the problem is that while there has been a very perceptible reduction in the cost of fish in the wholesale trade, that reduction does not seem to reach down to the retail trade. Everybody in the wholesale trade will tell us that the cost of fish is so much lower than it was, that many fish merchants have incurred very heavy losses, but the price to the consumer in the retail shop does not vary very much.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: With reference to the transportation of fish to the retailer from the sea, is there a refrigerator service provided for in the minister's estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Is there any increase for that so as to enlarge the service? That is one of the things that Canada requires more than anything else.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I will come to that in a moment, if the hon. member will wait.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: For the inland trade of the Dominion of Canada it is very important that refrigeration on express cars be provided. I do not think the fresh fish business can be properly undertaken and the inland market supplied unless we have a better system of transportation by express. In the winter season the goods are shipped in a frozen condition, and after being in a heated car for twenty-four hours they arrive at Montreal and Toronto in an almost unsaleable condition, if they have to be kept any time. The moment the frost comes out. of frozen fish, the fish should be immediately consumed; otherwise, it deteriorates in value. I do not think the transportation of frozen fish by express can be undertaken in less than carload lots unless some refrigeration is provided. To encourage the transportation of fish from the sea coast to our inland cities there should be express transportation every day in the week. When it comes to delivering fish by freight in carload lots the fish can be landed in good order in Toronto in the summer season, but in the winter season you cannot bring a box of fish from the seaboard to Toronto and deliver it in good condition. In the summer the fish is packed in ioe, and even if the ice melts, it is not very material, but even in the summer season there should be some portion of the car which could be cooled by salt and ice, and then the fish would arrive in much better condition than it does at the present time.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Are these salaries fixed by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Under the re-classification they will be.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: But they are not now? What salaries do you expect to pay to these inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I do not know what the re-classification will provide. I have in mind myself what would foe a fair salary, but the fixing of the salary is outside my jurisdiction. We shall have to wait and see in what class the officers are put.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I have been informed by some of the inspectors that when a guardian is to be appointed tenders for

the position are invited, through notice being put up in the different districts. These tenders are sent to Ottawa, where the selection is made. I submit that it would be difficult for the minister or any of his officers, unless they had some private information, to select a guardian for the district, of Cape North, for instance, in the county of Victoria, if half a dozen or more applications came in from that district from men all of whom were worthy citizens and would discharge the duties of the office equally well. Perhaps the minister will explain how the right person to be appointed is determined when only one man is to be selected out of a dozen applicants.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
The commission
form their opinion as to the proper man to select, largely, I presume, upon the recommendation of the local overseer or the inspector of fisheries for the district, they are not bound by that recommendation, but it is always passed on to them.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I do not think
that is the way in which it is being done, but if the minister says so, I do not like to contradict him. I think it would be a very good arrangement if the local fishery officer had absolute power to appoint his own men without interference from the department in any way. If he is made responsible for the district of which he is overseer and can select his own men, much more efficient service will be rendered than if the appointments are made for political reasons as they have been in the past. Is it a fact that there is no interference on the part of the department in making these appointments, and that the local fishery officer has been informed that he has absolute power to make the appointment, and that the department will stand behind that appointment when it is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
The hon. member
is quite right. The Civil Service Commission was so congested with business during the past year that the guardians were appointed by the local officers. I quite agree with my hon. friend that the way he suggests is the proper way and in so far as I have any influence it shall be used in that direction.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Are we then to understand that in future the rule will be that the fishery officer for the district will make these appointments independent of the department and of the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: No, I am sorry to say. If a guardian is wanted for less than thirty days the local officer can make the appointment, but if the appointment is for a longer time the position must be advertised, the local officer makes his recommendation to Ottawa, and it is passed on to the Civil Service Commission, who make the appointment.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: How is the Civil Service Commission to decide who is the best man when there are half a dozen applications for the position? I could understand how the local officer could pick the right man, but how the Civil Service Commission can do it is difficult for me to understand, when the applicants live a thousand miles away and the Commission knows nothing about them. Will the minister explain how it is done?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Before the Civil Service Commission took over the making of appointments, I stated on the floor of this House, last year when my Estimates were up, that I intended to leave all local appointments to the chief fishery officer in the various districts. Now, when there are several applicants for the same position, the local officer makes his recommendation to the Fisheries Department here as to the one he thinks most competent for the position, that recommendation is passed on to the Civil Service Commission, and as a rule is acted on by them, although they are not bound to do so.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
When last year the Minister of Marine and Fisheries promised a reduction in the number of fishery inspectors or guardians we on this side of the House gave him a well merited meed of applause. The 'minister has succeeded in doing what he said he would do. The House and the country should feel grateful to him, and I am sure they both do.
But the minister brings before the Committee to-day an item in his Estimates providing for an increase over last year of $100,000. I have listened very carefully to the discussion which is taking place to-night but have not been able to satisfy myself that the minister has made out a case for this increase. He shows us that in one substantial portion of this item he has effected a diminution in the personnel of the section of his department and an increase in salaries, which I think is perfectly right. I think that the public will be best served by having fewer and better paid officials. That is good business and common sense, and is, I am sure, what we want on both sides of the House. The

minister was kind enough to refer to me and my desire to protect the consumer. He said that he as well as myself had an eye to the consumer all the time. It is true he has an eye to the consumer, perhaps in the hope that the consumer's prosperity will enable him to get a little increase in price for what he has to sell to him. On this side of the House I protect the consumer in the hope of seeing that he gets his goods at a little lower price. But we are both thinking of the consumer, and both hope to see him happy and prosperous. Seriously speaking, however, I would like to have the minister establish his case for this increase of $100,000; because it is a truism-it is trite and tiresome but I must emphasize the fact-that we have to cut our financial coat according to our financial cloth in this country, and there has been no attempt on the part of the Government to cut down the Estimates, as far as I have been able yet to perceive. It seems to me that the ordinary expenses of this country are going to be more than they were last year, and I think we are in a very serious position.
Mr. iBALiLANTYNE :	I want to assure
the hon. member that I have no wares to sell. I formerly was in business, and when I get through with political life I shall devote all my time 'to tmy farming interests. Possibly, therefore, I have more interest in the consumer than the hon. member for Brome. But I want to say, with regard to the item, that the hon. member is quite right in asking for a little more information than I have given. The fishery service has been, I would not say deplorably weak, but it has been weak, and we are going to increa'se salaries of all those engaged in the fisheries of 'Canada. We shall engage fewer people and pay .them better salaries. Then the patrol service has to be increased also, but I have an eye to the expenditure and hope to get a Bill through the House that will allow me to increase the revenue of Canada to the extent of $262,000. So that I trust there will be no deficit in administering the fisheries when the present fiscal year is closed. I am doing my best to reduce the cost as far. as possible, and to increase the revenue and the efficiency at the same time. While the amount may seem large, I would like hon. members to realize the fact that the service was allowed to run down a little during the years of the war and we are now strengthening it. For this purpose we have to have more money for increases in salaries for fishery officers and also for patrol ser-
vice. I can go into details of the patrol service if it is necessary. The money is also required in connection with oyster culture. With regard to the patrol service, in order that hon. members may have some idea of the extent of this work I may say that we have 38 boats that are owned by the department and 18 that are hired. On the Atlantic coast there are 15 owned by the department and 9 hired; on the Pacific, 22 owned by the department and 9 hired; on (Lake Winnipeg. 1 owned by the department. These boats are engaged in preventing illegal fishing and are distinct from fisheries protection cruisers. I do not know that I can give more information than this, but if the money is voted we shall see that it is honestly disbursed.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Is it the intention to improve or further develop the fishing industry in the lakes in the Prairie Provinces? In the northern parts of these provinces we have some very large lakes and almost an unlimited supply of fish. And in view of the fact that these lakes are situated so near some of the cities which at present are showing signs of unrest, due no doubt to the high cost of living, it might be well to devote some attention to the possibilities of further developing this industry.
Mr. BAILLANiTYNE: I am glad that the hon. member has drawn attention to this matter, for we are certainly going to do everything we can in regard to our Great Lakes.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Will the money that is to be spent on oyster culture be devoted to patrol work, or in what way is it to be expended?
MV. BALLAXTYNE:	There are three
reasons why we want the money. We intend to increase the salaries of all officials, and we want it for the patrol service and also for oyster culture.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: In what way is the money to be spent in connection with oyster culture?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: On the recommendation of Mr. Ernest Kemp, who is a specialist on oysters, it is intended to keep the public beds in proper condition. For this purpose he has to have a boat. It will also afford information and advice to those going into private oyster culture; and, further, the Biological Board will assist very materially in a scientific way.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Can the minister say what proportion of the item will be used for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Between $6,000 and

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The fisheries officer in the county of Gloucester died two or three months ago. The Civil Service Commission called for applications, and I know that a number of applications have been sent in. Has the appointment been made yet, and if co, who has been appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
The appointment 'has not yet 'been made but the matter is now before the commission.
i Mr. CAHILL: It would 'be interesting to know how much of this money is to be spent on salaries, patrol service, oyster culture, and so on. The. Committee would like to have an idea of what the different phases of this work cost, and what ds the cost of the increase of the salaries to officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Salaries and disbursements for fishery officers in 1916-17 .amounted to $305,000.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: How much is it now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I cannot say exactly now what the increase will be because we have to go carefully over the list of officers and see what increases in salaries they ought to receive. We have not yet done so. We are asking for the appropriation first and will carefully go over the list of officers afterwards.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Will each officer get a share of the general increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission will settle the wages. I hope there will be a general increase, because the fishery officers are very much underpaid at the present time. I hope that when the Civil Service Commission finally settle the matter they will give to these good and efficient officers, and on merit, the increase in salary they are entitled to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: There are a great many officers in different parts of the country- I think they are called commissioners-who have a whole county, or more, to look after. They receive a small salary and their travelling disbursements are paid. Would the minister take the four counties of Cape Breton and tell us the salaries of the different officers there and how their travelling expenses compare with their salaries? Per-[DOT] haps I should not trouble the minister to give the comparison for the whole island of Cape Breton, but let him take one county and give us some idea as to how these accounts stand as between salary and travelling expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman has reference to overseers, and in Inverness county there are eight. In Eastern Harbour the overseer gets a yearly salary of $120, and is allowed ten cents a mile for travelling expenses. In Kingsville, Mr. McLellan gets $50; in Pleasant Bay, Mr. McIntosh gets $75; and in Port Hood, Mr. John A. McDougall gets $150. These are overseers, not guardians.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The minister has given the salaries. I also wanted the amount paid these officers for travelling expenses, to see how the two amounts compare.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The many hundreds of overseers are allowed ten cents a mile for travelling expenses. I will endeavour to furnish the amount of travelling expenses, but I am sorry I have not the information before me at present.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I am not very particular about it, because I had occasion to make a private inquiry into the subject a couple of years ago, and I find that while the salaries are very small the accumulation of travelling expenses is getting very high. Some years ago I suggested to the minister that it would be far better for the country, and in the interest of honesty and integrity on the part of the officials, that they should be paid a fixed salary and do away with the pernicious system of inviting them to pad their accounts so as to get moneys to which they are not entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I quite agree with the hon member that the system is not a good one, and is liable to be abused in just the manner he states. However, we intend to do away with the system, and to give these fishery overseers a fixed amount for travelling expenses each year, a sum that would be fair and reasonable according to the district which they are covering-possibly about $200 per annum. The present system is open to criticism as the hon. gentleman has very well stated, and a dishonest fishery overseer could pad his travelling expenses. I will not say it has been done, but the possibility of doing so exists, and the system will be changed.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I should like to get details if I can in regard to this item, which seems to be divided into three heads: Salaries and disbursements of fishery officers and guardians; fisheries patrol service; and oyster culture. I would like the minister to tell the Committee how much was spent under each head last year, and how much he estimates is going to be spent under

each head this year; also how many officers he had under the first head last year, and how many he expects to employ under the same head this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Under the heading of Salaries and Disbursements of Fishery Overseers, there was expended last year $305,000, and on the fisheries patrol service $190,000. The number of fishery guardians in 1917-1918 was 806, and this year the number is 392. The overseers in 1917-18 numbered 134, and we hope to greatly reduce them next year. The number of inspectors in 1917 was 24 and in 1918, 21. As to how we are going to divide the expenditure under the increase that we have asked for, that is a matter which will have to be determined in detail later on.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: What about oyster culture?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The expenditure for this purpose last year was $6,000.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: How much will it be this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: As far as we can tell it will not be much more during the coming year than it was last year.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I think we would make better headway if we took the items in the order they appear, and when we reach the item of fish breeding establishments I shall be glad to answer the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: There is no item relating to lobsters at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Hatcheries will
come under vote I have referred to.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I do not wish to be too persistent in regard to this item. But the minister told us that last year certain sums were allocated to salaries and to fisheries patrol service. Last year he asked $500,000, and this year he expects to spend $600,000 on oyster culture. That is increasing the vote by $100,000. I Would like to know which of the items get the increase. The
minister ought to be able to give us some idea of what these increases are going to be in each branch of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: As far as the oyster beds are concerned, as they are controlled by the provincial governments, that will explain why'the Federal authorities do not intend to spend any more than $600,000. I have as clearly as possible indicated that the $100,000 is for the salaries of the fishery officers and the patrol service; but to get down to the actual details of how much is for the patrol service and how much for the fishery officers is something I could not do until we had actually gone into the whole matter in detail. The first thing I must do is to try and get the members of the committee to give me $100,000 and then we will distribute it under these three headings. I could not tell to a dollar how much is going to be allocated to the patrol service and how much to the officers.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Tell us to $10,000.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I would expect the Fisheries Department to make a calculation of the amount of money needed. It is extraordinary that they should make up their minds to ask for $100,000 and yet not know what they are going to do with the money. That is not the business way of voting money. In a business concern, for instance, a bank, if salaries of the officers were to be increased, and $100,000 was required for that purpose,' the directors would have a statement and would know just why the amount was required and what was going to be done with it. But it appears that in the fisheries office a lump sum of $100,000 is asked for, and afterwards the officials are going to consider what they will do with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The hon. member is quite right. I have been in business myself and know exactly how a body of shareholders would question a proposed increase of $100,000. They would want to know first of all what the directors were going to do with it. If I told them it was for fisheries patrol and for fishery officers they would naturally inquire further how much we expected to spend on increased patrols and how much on increased salaries. In round figures, as the hon. member has asked, it would be $60,000 for patrols and $40,000 for salaries. That is not absolutely accurate, but it is what we estimate it will be.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: What is the cause of the great increase of $60,000 in patrols?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Because the service has been allowed to run down, due to the

war, we have not had a sufficient protective service. Now that the war is over we are increasing the number of patrol vessels and officers to give the protection that we think the fisheries ought to have. We were not able to do that during war time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The coast lines of Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia comprise a great many miles, and I do not see how one man can travel that distance during the short season of fishing and carry on this work with any degree of efficiency. If he had the whole year it would be different; but the fishing in the Maritime Provinces begins about the middle of May and ends some time in August, and one man could not inspect all the different-fishery points during that period. I assume that the inspector will be supposed to examine the packs of lobsters, to see how the work is carried on in the lobster factories, to ascertain how the guardians are doing their work, and so on. It is absolutely impossible for one man to do that work. If it is necessary at all to have such an official there should be more than one; but I am not in favour of the idea, because if the right men are locally selected to do the work of fishery officers there will be no need of any one to oversee the work. The money that the minister expects to spend on this official would produce better results if given to local officers-not to guardians, but to inspectors and other officials throughout the several provinces. If he increased their salaries and imposed greater burdens upon them he would get more efficiency from his officers and better results generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I quite understand that it would be impossible for this officer to visit in a short time all the various fishery points in the Maritime Provinces, but he will do so gradually. We shall try to get a man who is familiar with conditions there and who will co-ordinate the work. According to the experience of the Chief Inspector of Fisheries in British Columbia, the move is a wise one. If one officer is not enough it may be necessary at the next -session of Parliament to ask for another; but I am hopeful that one officer will be able to handle all the work. The inspectors in the Maritime Provinces now report to Ottawa; the intention is to have them report to the Chief Inspecting Officer for the Maritime Provinces and thus co-ordinate the work.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I want to mention a request that has been sent to me at vari-
[Mr. BaUantyne.1
ous times by farmers living along the St. Mary river in Nova Scotia. Some years ago these farmers had the right to set nets once or twice a week half way across the river for the purpose of catching salmon for their own use. They appreciated this privilege, which had been enjoyed by their forefathers for generations. But the department decided that no more net fishing for salmon should be allowed in that river. Now, the farmer has not time to use a fly to catch salmon, as the sportsmen do. I sympathize with the minister's idea that the fishing in .that river should be preserved; but the question is whether we are succeeding in doing it by our present method. The result of the present rigid method is that many of the people in that vicinity are turned into law-breakers. They take the ground that the salmon belongs to them, not to the sportsmen, because the river passes through their farms; that the right to catch these fish as I have described is an ancient right which they had for a long time and which should not have been taken away from them.. They satisfy their consciences in this way, and they break the law by going out at night to catch the salmon. I do not believe it would injure -the fishing in the river if once or twice a week, they were allowed to set their nets in certain places half way across the river and the law was rigidly enforced against any one who would sweep the river at night or violate the regulations. That is the proposal they have made to me, and their request would seem to be reasonable. I understand that that has been done in some rivers in New Brunswick. If it is true that farmers along certain rivers in New Brunswick are allowed to set nets under certain regulations, and if that practise is not injuring the fishing in those localities, I would like- the minister to consider the advisability of extending a similar privilege to the farmers along the banks of the St. Mary river.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.

Mr. CQP.P:	I was not in the House a

speechtext:
If the cultivation and protection of oysters is of any importance, the amount the minister is devoting to the work is very small. I hold in my hand a report made to the minister 'by some official of the department, and I notice that on page 17 it states:
The position of the oyster industry in the Maritime Provinces is an extremely unsatisfactory one. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: Is there not some legislation pending in connection, with this inspection? If it is the intention of the minister to press that legislation through Parliament this session I should like some further explanation about it, although I may not be quite in order in bringing up the matter on this item. The compulsory inspection of the fisheries is rather a disagreeable task to impose upon the fishermen in different parts of the country. This legislation. I speak of was before the House in the absence of the minister, and there was considerable opposition to it as far as it advanced, and I should like the minister to consider well before pressing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: We consulted all the interests, and the majority of them were in favour of making the inspection of pickled fish compulsory. The matter has also been discussed with the various associations that have called upon me, and as far as I know, this legislation is being introduced to meet their wishes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I pointed out to the Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries when this legislation was up earlier in the session that the greatest possible difficulties and legal entanglements might result from tt's inspection. A man may put up 500 barrels of herring down in northern Victoria county, where there are large fishing interests. He believes it to be No. 1 herring and sells it for No. 1 to some concern in Halifax. There is no provision as to where the fish shall be inspected. The man in Halifax who buys this No. 1 herring without saying a word that he is going to have, it inspected may get an inspector to say that it is only No.
2 or No. 3 herring. Then the fat is in the fire, and there will be all kinds of trouble. The fish is sold and beyond the reach of the man who had it in his possession. If there is to be an inspection, it should take place at the place where the fish is packed; otherwise there will be all manner of trouble be-

tween the seller and the buyer, and the fishermen as a rule are not sufficiently rwell off to stand the expense of a lawsuit. There are many other reasons why compulsory inspection should not be pressed upon the people just now. There may be some large sellers of fish who are in favour of compulsory inspection, but it is not the man who buys from the fisherman all along the coast and sells again that I am thinking of, but the small man who put up small quantities of fish and who is now getting along first-rate and has been, and those before him, for the last seventy-five or a hundred years. I am not in favour of imposing fresh duties and further obligations and compulsions by law upon such a man. He has enough to contend with already. He has to fight his way into the Atlantic and battle with the elements in order to catch the fish, and after he has caught it I am not in favour of putting any more embarrassing obligations upon him unless there is real necessity for it. So far we have been putting up very excellent fish in the province of Nova Scotia;
I have heard no great complaints. It is to the interest of every fishermen to put up good fish, for he is competing with his neighbours who are putting up good fish. That is the result of local competition, which has been doing very well. Unless the minister finds that the ordinary fisherman is satisfied to have these new obligations imposed upon him, I would not be in favour of imposing them. If he is willing to submit to this inspection, that is his business, but so far I have had no evidence of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Will the minister deal with the question of the propagation of lobsters?
Mr. BALLAiNTYNE:	I carefully considered the subject before those fourteen lobster hatcheries were closed by the Government, and consulted a number of men interested in the business, both business men and scientific men; and from the information I gathered I did not see thait they were of any practical use. The fishermen take the lobsters and after brushing off the berries the eggs are taken to the hatchery. We found that the propagation in the hatchery was only about 30 per cent, but when the propagation occurred from the female berried lobster in the natural way it was 100 per cent. The small fry are exposed in the sea, whether they come from the lobster hatchery or whether the eggs are exuded in the natural way. While the lobster hatcheries were costing the Government considerable money we found that instead of being of service to the industry they were the reverse. For that reason I recommended that the hatcheries should be closed. But I was very careful in the matter. As the hon. member said, I waited for a year, and sought advice from every available source that could be of assistance. We have sold three of the lobster hatcheries, one at Shippegan for $610, another at House Harbour for $760, and another at Canso. For the Biological Board for scientific investigation purposes we are retaining the hatcheries at Arichat, Antigonish, Bay-view, Charlottetown and Port Daniel. The remaining hatcheries are offered for sale: Inverness Harbour, Little Bras d'Or, Isaac's Harbour, Georgetown, Shemogue and Buctouche. I am not an authority on lobsters and all I could do was to consult those interested in the business in the Maritime Provinces. I was largely guided by the report of Professor Knight, and if it is a fact that there was a propagation of only 30 per cent in the lobster hatcheries as compared with 100 per cent in the natural way, it was conclusive evidence that the hatcheries wpre not performing any useful service to the country and that the lobster interests would be best served without them.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: What proof has the minister that there was 100 per cent propagation in the natural way?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I am only quoting Professor Knight's opinion.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Professor Prince was opposed to the step taken by the minister and he is our authority on this matter. I do not know who Professor Knight is, but I am quite sure that no man will say that there was 100 per cent natural propagation because that is impossible of demonstration, and if any professor makes that statement he is "talking through his hat." As regards 'the 30 per cent propagation, I think that if we succeeded in securing that percentage we were doing very well. The number of eggs on a lobster is something enormous. It runs up into the millions; at all events hundreds of thousands. I cannot remember the number, but I know it is large. According to the reports of the department there were hundreds of millions of young lobsters put into the water every year from these hatcheries, and the propagation of 30 per cent was very good. They were lively looking little lobsters when they were put .out, but whether they would live afterwards was a matter of doubt and that was the question that the department never seemed to have the enterprise to investigate. These lobster fry were siphoned out on the water some three miles from the coast and after that they were allowed to shift for themselves. They were very small and I have seen them about the size of a mosquito. The theory of the scientists was that they floated on the surface for some time until they developed, when they sank and crawled on the bottom. As far as I know the department has never made an investigation to discover whether or not they survived and it was a controversy among the fishermen as to whether these young lobsters survived when they were put into the ocean. That was the question which should have been Ascertained by the department and it is surely capable of being ascertained. What I complain of chiefly is the fact that the minister undertook this matter without consulting those members interested in the fisheries. In a question of this kind, which is not a political but a business iquestion, and on which there cannot be any difference between the Government and the Opposition as regards the proper administration, is it not curious that although, we have a Fisheries Committee sitting, the minister should-
Mr. BALLANT1NE: The hon. member will surely remember that I appeared before the Fisheries Committee last year and went very fully into this matter. As to whether or not it was a good thing to do 
that is purely a scientific question. Professor Knight and the Biological Board, which is composed of some of the most eminent university men in 'Canada, including Professor Prince, strongly recommended the step, and I can only act on the advice of such eminent scientific authorities as I have quoted. But I remember having appeared before the Committee myself and having spent half an hour or more discussing this very subject.
Mr. J. II. SINCLAIR: That is true. I had not the pleasure of being present when the minister was before the Committee. But there were several meeting of the Committee, and if a vote had been taken the action of my hon. friend would, I think, have been almost unanimously condemned. The Chairman of the Committee asked us not to pass a resolution condemning the action of the department without hearing the minister. The minister appeared before the Committee subsequently and made a statement, but whether he convinced the Committee or not no one. knows; he did not give the Committee an opportunity of meeting again and coming to a decision. I understood that the minister stated that he would call a meeting of the fishermen and fish packers, and people interested in the fisheries in the Maritime Provinces and submit the question to them. He did call a meeting last year at Halifax, but he has not told us what the decision was. I was at the meeting, but I do not remember of any decision having been arrived at in regard to this question, and I think that if it had been put to a vote of the meeting there would have been a considerable difference of opinion. But we have a number of men in the House representing the Maritime Provinces and i would like to know what we are here for. Is our advice not to be listened to? Are we not to be consulted on a question like this, but is some professor up in Kingston to decide whether lobster hatcheries in the Maritime Provinces are to be closed or kept open? My complaint is that the minister, without consulting members of Parliament who are interested in the fisheries, decided to close the lobster hatcheries and to sell them. He says he has sold one in my own constituency that was doing splendid work.
I do not care what he received for it if he made ai'bad bargain by selling it. Their advice was ignored, and if the 'Committee had been consulted in my opinion they would have decided against the action of' the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman scarcely does me justice. He criticises me

for not being present at the meeting in Halifax, when at -that very time I was attending the Imperial Conference in London, England.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I am not complaining about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
With regard to these
matters not being put before members of Parliament, I fully agree with the hon. gentleman. This whole matter was referred to the Fisheries Committee, but, unfortunately, ministers are so driven by the pressure of public business that they cannot attend these committee meetings as often as they would like. For instance, a meeting of the Fisheries Committee was called for this morning at eleven o'clock. How many appointments had I at that hour? There was a very important meeting of -the Cabinet- taking place at eleven o'clock and I was asked to be there. A very large delegation o.f labour men representing the shipyards in the East wished to meet me at eleven o'clock. Then there was the meeting of the Fisheries Committee at the same time. Well, I chose to meet the labour men, and, therefore, was unable, much to my regret, to be present at the Fisheries Committee meeting. I would like to attend all the meetings, but if any men have cause for striking it is the ministers of the Crown. Talk about working eight hours a day; we are driven from early morning until the present advanced hour of the nightj and it is quite probable that two or three gentlemen will still want to see us after we reach our hotel. I have always referred these matters to -the Fisheries Committee, and this subject was thoroughly discussed there. My good friend from Shelburne and Queen's found some fault with me a year ago for not attending a committee meeting. I really could not do so because there were so many other matters pressing for my attention. However, I am always glad to be present whenever I can do so, and that has always been my wish.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: Did the minister get the consent, or the approval, of the Fisheries Committee for -the course he has taken in this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Yes, as far as I
understood it. I did not hear any gentleman there opposing the suggested action, and I certainly understood that I had the unanimous approval of the Committee, after going into the matter very fully. As to the Halifax Convention, I was not there, but the department was represented by the
superintendent of fisheries, Mr. Found. He says this matter was not discussed at all; the discussion there was about the regulations with regard to the fishing of lobsters. If my memory serves me right, and I have a fairly good memory in regard to past events, the Fisheries Committee gave me their unanimous approval.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I question very much if any resolution was passed on the subject by the Fisheries Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Logg-ie) was present and I regret very much he is not here to-night.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The attitude ol the Fisheries Committee was quite different before the minister did them the honour of conferring with them, and if they had been allowed to pass a resolution on the subject it would certainly have been in opposition to what the minister has done. My point is that after the meeting in Halifax the Fisheries Committee should have been called together and the members from the Maritime Provinces consulted before the minister took the step he did. I concur in what my hon. friend (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) has said with respect to the disappearance of the lobster hatcheries. The lobster hatchery at Shippigan, in my county, has been sold. I had expected that at the clo-se of the last session of Parliament, according to the understanding of the Fisheries Committee, some offi-

eial would visit my county in reference to this matter. However, no one came to the county of Gloucester, but nevertheless the lobster hatchery there has been sold, and 1 presume for a song.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: The firm got a good bargain that time. Now what are we going to do in regard to the propagation of lobster?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext: I am not an authority on lobster propagation. It is purely a scientific question, not a business one, and the biological board is composed of the brightest scientific men we could get throughout Canada, including Professor Prince. That board recommended to the Minister of Fisheries that it was in the interest of the lobster industry to close the hatcheries. I did not take scientific advice merely, 'but sought information elsewhere, and the matter was thoroughly threshed out before the Fisheries Committee. I did not know that the Committee paid me such deference that they would not express their opinions freely if I happened to be present at their meetings. I appreciate the honour, but I hope that in future when I attend their meetings they will have no hesitancy whatever in expressing their minds frankly. If all the members of that Committee remained silent on this question a year ago when I was present at their meeting, I cannot be blamed for taking that as consenting to what was proposed. As far as I can tell the move is a wise one and in the interests of the lobster industry, but it is purely a scientific question, and I would not attempt to offer any opinion on it myself.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
May I be permitted to proffer advice which I believe to be sound. The lobster hatcheries along our shores have disappeared, and there are now only two measures left for the maintenance of that fishery-maintenance of the close season and limitation of the size of lobsters taken. The close season may have served somewhat in the past, but really the maintenance of the size of the lobsters is the only salvation for the industry in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
Mr. *BALLANTYNE: And the protection of the berried lobster as well.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
Last year, or two years ago, the Minister of Fisheries abolished the regulation as to the size of the lobster that could be caught and any lobsters at all were allowed to be brought in. It is pretty difficult to enforce such a regulation, and the only way is to make the packer himself responsible for the size of every lobster he buys-whether he buys from independent fishermen or whether he takes the catch of fishermen who work for him by the day. The packer ought to be made responsible for every lobster that goes into his boiler. It is better to spend a few dollars in that way, and have the guardians loou carefully into the character of the lobster pack at each factory, than to adopt regulations which would not foe enforced. I do not wish to indulge in any lengthy observations at this late hour of the evening, but I repeat that the only salvation for the lobster industry in the Gulf of St. Lawrence is to maintain the size of the lobsters. For the last twenty-five years they have not been allowed to grow in those waters. In the case of the Bay of Fundy districts the lobsters must be nine and a half or ten inches in size to find a market in the United States, and owing to that requirement their size has been maintained, notwithstanding the immense amount of lobster fishing that is done there.
We were told that our fishermen and packers would not be allowed to take small lobsters so that in a few years big lobsters would be again plentiful. I have always contended that under the conditions prevailing during the last ten years we should have stopped taking lobsters from the gulf of St. Lawrence for two or three years at least, and should have divided the district into two portions so that the fishing would not be too much interrupted. I submit those considerations to the minister, and I believe he will find that they are sound and ought to be put into practice.

subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend from Gloucester has been quite fair to the packers, because he must realize that in the Maritime Provinces at least, if not all over Canada, the lobster packers have been only putting three-quarters of a pound of lobster in a pound can, and in that way have been conserving the lobster.
I do not know which of these items contains the expenses of conducting fishery investigations, but I have in my hand a very valuable report on the lobster fisheries,
,

and I want to draw the attention of the Committee to it. I find one clause in it in regard to the canning of lobsters in the province of New Brunswick. It is stated that there are 660 shippers in various parts of the province, and that their output amounted to 195,993 cases of 48 pounds each. I understand, Mr. Chairman, that there is only 36 pounds in a case of lobsters, and I contend that this report is absolutely wrong and misleading to the public when it states the measure of the amount of lobsters taken in the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.

Item 230, development of deep sea fisheries, was allowed to stand. Some hon. gentlemen who are not in the House to-night wish to discuss various fishery matters, and therefore I would not wish the minister to be in any particular hurry about bringing this up for some days.
I have in mind that the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) will be away for ten days or so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: FISHERIES ESTIMATES-STATEMENT BY HON. MR. BALLANTYNE.
speechtext:
There is no hon. member that I would like to oblige so much as the hon. member for Lunenburg, but owing to the amount of business that remains to be transacted-and we all hope the House will prorogue by the end of June -I could not promise to leave this item to stand over for ten days. I would like to finish it to-morrow.
Progress reported.
